statement: In people who use several drugs, tested by one research group at University College London at parties, nightclubs or squat parties within 30 minutes of saying they had taken ketamine, ketamine use that night compared with no ketamine that night is associated with much lower scores on most memory and thinking tests and with strong self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like experiences and bodily and perceptual changes; three days later most of these differences had gone, but some memory differences remained and, in one of the two studies, dissociation and psychosis-like scores were still higher; these studies cannot attribute what remained to the night of use. On the night (Curran & Morgan, 2000), 20 people who had taken ketamine, against 19 peers from the same settings who had not (all 20 in the ketamine group and 17 of the 19 peers had also smoked cannabis that night), recalled 3.83 against 8.61 ideas of a short story (maximum 21), correctly judged 42.35 against 76.05 sentences in 2 minutes, made 10.8 against 22.37 correct serial-seven subtractions and named 11.20 against 17.74 category members; an implicit (word-stem) memory task did not differ. They rated dissociation at 44.00 against 5.47, and impaired memory at 72.40 against 16.63, bodily numbness at 60.30 against 6.16 and altered time perception at 59.60 against 9.79 on ratings from no symptom to severe symptom. In a second sample with no group free of ketamine (Curran & Monaghan, 2001; 18 people who used ketamine more than twice a month and 19 who used it less), both groups scored similarly low on story recall and category naming on the night (although letter fluency was already lower in the more frequent group, 10.39 against 17.42), rated very high dissociation (34.83 and 39.26) and rated themselves more sedated and more anxious than three days later. Three days later, at home (by their own account no one had taken ketamine on days 1 to 3, although 36% of the 2000 ketamine group had taken more after the first test that night and everyone in that study had used alcohol or cannabis on days 1 and 2), the 2000 groups no longer differed in serial-seven subtractions (21.30 against 23.37) or digit-cancellation times, and their symptom ratings (11 of 14 with group × day interactions) were similar apart from a trend to more self-rated memory problems in the ketamine group (26.45 against 11.95); in the second sample dissociation had fallen to 4.56 and 3.47, while the more frequent group still rated more impaired memory (35.94 against 15.42) and concentration (33.11 against 12.74) than the less frequent group, rated more sedation on both days and more often reported alcohol on the day of the retest (8 of 18 against 4 of 19, timing not stated). Story recall was still lower in the 2000 ketamine group (7.75 against 10.18) but did not differ from the comparison group's first-night score, which the authors attribute to missed practice after poor memory of the first session; category naming and sentence judging were lower on both days, which fits differences that predate the night, after-effects or missed practice: the paper's practice check found no difference for category naming, and its check for sentence judging, printed as p<0.009, gives p ≈ 0.04 on the editors' recalculation from its own table, about the same as for category naming. In the second sample, by day 3 the group that used ketamine less often recalled about twice as much of the story as the group that used it more often (9.16 against 4.56), whose immediate recall was no better than on the night (its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39); the more frequent group had less schooling. The studies disagree on whether dissociation and psychosis-like scores stay raised: three days after use they were still higher in the 2000 ketamine group than in its comparison group (17.75 against 5.37; 62.35 against 26.42), but low in both groups of the second sample; the same team describes a laboratory study in which healthy volunteers given ketamine did not differ from volunteers given placebo three days later (second-hand, as described by Morgan et al., 2009). In the 2000 study a single depression rating did not differ between groups on either day, and depression scores on an anxiety and depression questionnaire were somewhat higher in the ketamine group on both days (the first rating covered the two days up to the test on the night) and below the range the authors call clinically significant, while anxiety did not differ. Neither study asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it. Use was self-reported and not tested, amounts and content are unknown, and the testers were not reported to be blind to group. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: At parties and clubs, people tested within half an hour of taking ketamine did far worse on memory and thinking tests than people there who had not taken it: they remembered less than half as much of a short story, for example. They felt strongly cut off from their body and surroundings, numb, and as if time had changed. Three days later, at home, their attention scores matched the other group's and most of these feelings had gone. Some memory scores were still lower; this may be because people remembered little of the first test and so had less practice, because of after-effects, or because the groups were different to begin with. One study found that feeling detached was still higher after three days; the other did not. In that other study, three days later, people who used ketamine more often rated their memory and concentration as worse than people who used it less often. What people took was never tested, and both studies come from one research team.
population: Young adults who use several drugs, recruited at private parties, nightclubs and squat parties by one research group at University College London and tested where they were using drugs: 20 who had taken ketamine that night and 19 who had not (Curran & Morgan, 2000); 18 who used ketamine more than twice a month and 19 who used it less, all of whom had taken it that night (Curran & Monaghan, 2001)
exposure: Ketamine taken that evening, by self-report, within 30 minutes before the first test; amount and content not verified
comparator: Peers from the same parties or club with little or no ketamine use who had not taken it that night (2000); in the 2001 sample no group without ketamine: people who used it twice a month or less against people who used it more often, and each group against itself three days later
outcome: Memory, thinking and attention test scores, and self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like (schizotypal) experiences, bodily and perceptual symptoms and mood, on the night of use and three days later
magnitude: Curran & Morgan (2000), 20 against 19, within 30 minutes of reported use (day 0) and 3 days later (day 3), means (SD): day 0 immediate story recall 3.83 (2.17) against 8.61 (2.57), delayed 2.48 (1.50) against 6.87 (3.32); sentences correctly judged 42.35 (13.33) against 76.05 (21.45); serial sevens 10.8 (6.56) against 22.37 (8.19); category fluency 11.20 (4.38) against 17.74 (5.39); letter fluency 16.00 (4.59) against 21.32 (5.42); cancellation time 69.90 (18.46) against 54.92 (11.66) s; word-stem targets 3.00 against 3.58 (no difference); standardized differences about 0.9 to 2.0 (editors' calculation). Dissociation 44.00 against 5.47 (day 0), 17.75 (SD 17.41) against 5.37 (day 3, p<0.008); schizotypal 87.40 against 33.37, 62.35 against 26.42 (p<0.001). Symptom ratings day 0: impaired memory 72.40 against 16.63, numbness 60.30 against 6.16, altered time 59.60 against 9.79; 11 of 14 ratings with group × day interactions; day 3 impaired memory 26.45 against 11.95 (trend, p<0.04). Day 3: serial sevens 21.30 against 23.37; cancellation 58.45 against 57.96 s; immediate recall 7.75 against 10.18; category fluency 14.85 against 19.68; sentences 63.30 against 79.11 (practice check printed p<0.009, editors' recalculation p ≈ 0.04). HADS depression 4.45 against 1.89 (day 0, covering the two days before) and 4.30 against 1.68 (day 3), below the 8–11 range. Curran & Monaghan (2001), 18 (13.53 days a month) against 19 (0.45 days a month): day 0 immediate recall 4.67 and 5.00, letter fluency 10.39 against 17.42, dissociation 34.83 and 39.26; day 3 dissociation 4.56 and 3.47, schizotypal 25.28 and 28.95 (no group differences); day 3 immediate recall 4.56 against 9.16 and delayed 4.39 against 8.05 (interaction F(1,35) = 13.5 and 6.7; the more frequent group's delayed recall was 3.11 on day 0), category fluency 14.06 against 18.95; day-3 ratings of impaired memory 35.94 against 15.42 and impaired concentration 33.11 against 12.74; alcohol on day 3 in 8 of 18 against 4 of 19.

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants and design, 1st paragraph (p. 577, continuing on p. 578); Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 578); Assessments › Cognitive tasks › Prose recall and Speed of comprehension test (p. 578); Assessments › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology, and Mood and subjective effects (p. 579)
evidence.extracted: Two groups of people who all used several drugs, recruited at private parties or a nightclub and aged 18 to 29: 20 who had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing, and 19 who had little or no previous ketamine use and had not taken it that evening. Both groups were tested on the night (day 0) in a small quiet room away from the music and again 3 days later (day 3) in their homes, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order; 7 more people tested once were not retested and 2 were discarded for taking drugs on the day of the second session. Story (prose) recall was scored in idea units, maximum 21, and the speed of comprehension test asked people to judge as many of 100 sentences as they could in 2 minutes. The self-ratings were an adapted dissociative states scale, a state schizotypal symptom questionnaire built for the study, a mood scale, 14 symptom ratings anchored at no symptom and severe symptom, and an anxiety and depression questionnaire rated for the last two days; no measure asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it.

evidence.locator: Table 1, day 0 columns (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Word-stem completion (p. 584)
evidence.extracted: On the night, means (SD), ketamine group against comparison group: immediate story recall 3.83 (2.17) against 8.61 (2.57) and delayed recall 2.48 (1.50) against 6.87 (3.32) idea units; letter fluency 16.00 (4.59) against 21.32 (5.42) words; category fluency 11.20 (4.38) against 17.74 (5.39); sentences judged on the speed of comprehension test 42.35 (13.33) against 76.05 (21.45); correct serial-seven subtractions 10.8 (6.56) against 22.37 (8.19); digit-cancellation time 69.90 (18.46) against 54.92 (11.66) seconds; word-stem completion targets 3.00 (1.95) against 3.58 (2.01), the one task without a group difference. Editors' calculation (pooled SD, n 20 and 19): standardized differences of about 0.9 to 2.0 on every task except word-stem completion, for example immediate recall g −1.97 (95% CI −2.74 to −1.21).

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 2) › Dissociative States Scale and Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire (p. 584, continuing on p. 585)
evidence.extracted: Self-ratings, ketamine group against comparison group, on the night and 3 days later: dissociation total 44.00 (13.98) against 5.47 (5.71), then 17.75 (17.41) against 5.37 (7.21) (group × day F(1,37) = 51.3; day-3 difference p<0.008); state schizotypal symptoms 87.40 (16.21) against 33.37 (21.71), then 62.35 (25.35) against 26.42 (20.45) (interaction F(1,37) = 14.0, p = 0.001; day-3 difference p<0.001); magical ideation on day 3 28.25 (12.75) against 11.00 (10.48). In the comparison group the correlations between the two days were 0.93 for dissociation and 0.94 for schizotypy.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (p. 582, printed sideways); Results › Mood and somatic measures › Subjective Effects Scale (p. 585, left column)
evidence.extracted: Symptom ratings on the night, ketamine group against comparison group: impaired memory 72.40 (19.58) against 16.63 (21.38), impaired concentration 66.40 (21.17) against 25.05 (24.57), bodily numbness 60.30 (25.10) against 6.16 (9.63), altered time perception 59.60 (28.37) against 9.79 (15.01), out-of-body experience 40.95 (31.77) against 3.37 (5.50). Of the 14 ratings, 11 showed group × day interactions and the groups were similar on day 3, apart from a trend (p<0.04) to more self-rated impaired memory in the ketamine group (26.45 (25.13) against 11.95 (16.83)). The depression rating showed no group, day or interaction effect (16.20 against 13.16 on the night, 22.80 against 11.95 on day 3).

evidence.locator: Table 1, day 3 columns (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Serial sevens and Digit cancellation task (p. 584)
evidence.extracted: Three days later, correct serial-seven subtractions were 21.30 (8.31) against 23.37 (8.37) and digit-cancellation times 58.45 (9.51) against 57.96 (9.44) seconds, the groups performing at the same level (group × day interactions F(1,37) = 13.6 and 15.0).

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks (Table 1) › Prose recall (p. 581, continuing on p. 583); Discussion › Cognitive effects, 5th paragraph (p. 586, right column)
evidence.extracted: Story recall on day 3 was still lower in the ketamine group: immediate 7.75 (2.08) against 10.18 (2.99), delayed 6.73 (2.55) against 9.76 (3.30) (immediate recall group × day F(1,37) = 7.55; delayed recall group and day effects without an interaction). The ketamine group's day-3 immediate recall did not differ significantly from the comparison group's first-night score, and the authors conclude that the day-3 recall differences likely reflect a lack of practice, because the drug impaired memory of the first session. Editors' observation from Table 1: the ketamine group's day-3 delayed recall (6.73) was close to the comparison group's first-night score (6.87).

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Category generation (p. 583, continuing on p. 584) and Speed of comprehension test (p. 584)
evidence.extracted: Category fluency was lower in the ketamine group on both days (group F(1,37) = 21.1; day 3 14.85 (3.08) against 19.68 (4.58)) without a group × day interaction, and its day-3 score did not differ significantly from the comparison group's first-night score. Sentences correctly judged were lower on both days (day 3 63.30 (16.04) against 79.11 (19.94); interaction F(1,37) = 28.9), and the ketamine group's day-3 score is reported as significantly below the comparison group's first-night score (p<0.009). Editors' calculation from Table 1 (independent t-test, pooled SD): this check gives t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04 for sentence judging, almost the same as for category fluency (t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046), which the paper reports as not significant (card sc_curran_2000, reporting issues).

evidence.locator: Procedure, 3rd paragraph (p. 578); Results › Demographics and drug use, 1st paragraph, and Reported drug use on day 0 (p. 579, continuing on p. 580); Reported general drug use, end of the paragraph (p. 581); Discussion, paragraph on methodological limitations (p. 588, left column)
evidence.extracted: Ketamine use was known only from what people said: hair samples were collected on day 3 but not analysed because the resources were not available, and drugs and amounts could not be confirmed. On the night, all 20 in the ketamine group and 17 controls had smoked cannabis, and 65% and 72% had drunk alcohol, more than 2 hours before testing; 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after testing but, by their own account, none on days 1 to 3; everyone reported alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1 and 2, at similar levels in the two groups, and none on day 3. University-level education: 15 of the ketamine group against 18 controls; 4 in the ketamine group and 1 control had been prescribed antidepressants in the past.

evidence.locator: Assessments › Mood and subjective effects (p. 579); Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Mood and somatic measures › Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (p. 585, left column)
evidence.extracted: On the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, rated for the last two days instead of the last week, depression scores were higher in the ketamine group on the night (4.45 (2.11) against 1.89 (1.29)) and 3 days later (4.30 (2.58) against 1.68 (1.29)) (group F(1,32) = 19.4), which the authors call low and well below the clinically significant range of 8–11; anxiety did not differ (7.05 to 7.85 in all four cells).

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants and design, 1st paragraph (p. 751); Assessments, Mood and subjective effects and Other assessments (pp. 752–753); Table 1 (p. 754)
evidence.extracted: A second sample of people who used several drugs, recruited at clubs and squat parties, all of whom reported taking ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing: 18 who used it more than twice a month and 19 who used it twice a month or less (reported days of use a month 13.53 (6.18) against 0.45 (0.80)), tested on the night (day 0) and 3 days later (day 3); there was no group without ketamine. The self-ratings were the same dissociation and schizotypy scales, a mood scale and 12 symptom ratings, with impulsivity and personality questionnaires on day 3; no measure asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it.

evidence.locator: Table 2 and Results › Cognitive assessments › Verbal fluency (p. 754); Results › Cognitive assessments › Serial sevens and digit cancellation, Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 3), and Mood and subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 755); Table 3 (p. 756); Table 4 (p. 757)
evidence.extracted: On the night both groups scored similarly low on story recall and category fluency: immediate story recall 4.67 (2.59) and 5.00 (3.66), category fluency 11.83 (4.32) and 12.58 (6.54), although letter fluency was already lower in the more frequent group (10.39 (6.01) against 17.42 (7.22)); dissociation was very high (34.83 (21.60) and 39.26 (25.32)) and so were state schizotypal scores (54.11 (30.22) and 53.58 (28.39)). Three days later dissociation (4.56 (6.35) and 3.47 (5.56)) and schizotypal scores (25.28 (19.80) and 28.95 (21.37)) had fallen in both groups (day effects F(1,35) = 78.1 and 48.2) with no group differences; serial sevens and cancellation improved in both groups (F(1,35) = 14.10 and 18.1) without group differences; all participants rated more sedation and both groups more anxiety on the night than on day 3 (F(1,35) = 41.8 and 9.33); and bodily numbness fell from 54.89 and 60.21 to 8.00 and 3.68.

evidence.locator: Results › Demographics and reported drug use, 1st paragraph, and Reported drug use on day 0 and day 3 (p. 753); Table 2 and Results › Cognitive assessments › Prose recall and Verbal fluency (p. 754); Category generation (p. 755); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 757, continuing on p. 758)
evidence.extracted: Three days later the group using ketamine twice a month or less recalled 9.16 (3.86) ideas immediately and 8.05 (4.05) after a delay, against 4.56 (1.96) and 4.39 (1.57) in the group using it more often, whose immediate recall was no higher than on the night (4.67 (2.59)), although its delayed recall rose from 3.11 (2.28) (immediate recall group × day F(1,35) = 13.5; delayed F(1,35) = 6.7, printed p<0.01); category fluency was 18.95 (4.45) against 14.06 (3.83) (interaction F(1,35) = 4.18, p<0.05); letter fluency was lower in the more frequent group on both days (10.39 against 17.42, then 14.00 against 22.10). Highest qualification, more frequent against less frequent group: degree 0 against 4, GCSE 12 against 5; all participants reported no ketamine between the two sessions; the authors say baseline differences between the groups cannot be ruled out. Editors' calculation: F(1,35) = 6.7 corresponds to p ≈ 0.014.

The authors note that the earlier study's ketamine group used ketamine on average 3.1 times a month, more than this study's less frequent group (0.45) and less than its more frequent group (13.5), yet only that group still had raised dissociation and schizotypal scores on day 3; they suggest a U-shaped relation with amount of use, or differences between the samples (the earlier one mainly from nightclubs and 75% university-educated, this one mainly from squat parties and 28%). Editors' check: the 28% cannot be derived from this paper's own education figures (no degree holders among 18 and 4 among 19; card sc_curran_2001, reporting issues).

The same research group states that healthy volunteers given ketamine in a controlled laboratory study did not differ from volunteers given placebo when tested 3 days later (their reference 9, a laboratory study not read here), and lists three explanations for lower scores in people who use ketamine tested a few days after use: after-effects of the recent dose, differences that predate use, and long-lasting effects.

evidence.locator: Results › Reported drug use on day 0 and day 3 (p. 753, right column); Results › Mood and subjective effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 755, right column); Table 3, mood factors, alertness (p. 756); Table 4 (p. 757)
evidence.extracted: On day 3, 15 participants reported cannabis (8 in the more frequent and 7 in the less frequent group) and 12 alcohol (8 and 4; 1 to 3 units), without a statement of whether this came before the retest. The more frequent group rated more sedation than the less frequent group on both days (alertness factor, group F(1,35) = 4.63, p<0.04; the authors read higher scores as more sedation) and more nausea (group F(1,35) = 5.37, p<0.05); on day 3 it rated more impaired concentration, 33.11 (26.84) against 12.74 (12.53) (group × day F(1,35) = 5.79, p<0.025), and more impaired memory, 35.94 (23.09) against 15.42 (18.00) (a group effect printed with the same statistic, F(1,35) = 5.79).

risk_of_bias.note: Groups were formed by what people chose to take that night; use was self-reported and never tested (hair collected but not analysed); the testers were not reported to be blind to group; alcohol and cannabis use between the sessions was neither controlled nor verified; the schizotypy questionnaire was built for the study and the dissociation scale used only its self-rated items; the ketamine group of the first study differed in education and past antidepressant use; several printed statistics do not match their tables (cards sc_curran_2000 and sc_curran_2001: ROBINS-E very high overall, high for the night-of-use contrast).

inconsistency.note: The two studies agree on the night of use and on the fading of attention deficits and dissociation by day 3, but disagree on whether dissociation and psychosis-like scores stay raised after three days, which the authors cannot explain.

indirectness.note: People who use ketamine tested where they use it, which is the population asked about; because amounts and content are unknown, the results cannot be tied to any amount.

imprecision.note: 20 and 19, and 18 and 19 people; the night-of-use differences are large and clear, but the day-3 differences sit near the limit of what samples this size can detect (card sc_curran_2000, power).

large_effect.note: Standardized differences on the night are about 1 to 2 (editors' calculation), but a large difference between small self-selected groups does not qualify for an upgrade (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Within the ketamine group of the first study the reported amount taken did not correlate with any cognitive or symptom score (card sc_curran_2000); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational field studies outside a laboratory start low (round brief; METHODS §6.3) and are rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (the day-3 findings) and imprecision, below the floor: very low. Strict reading: the direction of the night-of-use differences is not in doubt, given their size, their reappearance in a second sample and the authors' report that they match laboratory studies of single doses, but their size and what remains on day 3 are very uncertain. Overlapping evidence: both studies come from one laboratory with the same test battery; the samples are distinct (20 and 19; 18 and 19), so the status is replicated by the same team, not replicated. The laboratory study of healthy volunteers three days after a dose is known here only from the same team's description, for which its papers cite two different laboratory reports (cards sc_morgan_2009 and sc_morgan_2004a, reporting issues), and is not counted.
